questions.title: Call Option Payoff and Breakeven
questions.prompt: Walk me through how a call option's payoff works at expiration. If I buy a call with a $50 strike for a $4 premium, and the stock settles at $57 at expiration, what's the payoff, what's my profit, and where exactly is breakeven?
questions.code:
Call payoff = max(S - K, 0)
Profit (buyer) = payoff - premium
Breakeven (long call) = K + premium
questions.modelAnswer: A long call's payoff at expiration is max(S - K, 0): if the stock finishes above the strike, the payoff equals the difference; if it finishes at or below the strike, the option expires worthless and the payoff is zero. Profit for the buyer is payoff minus the premium paid, since the premium is a sunk cost paid upfront regardless of outcome. With S=$57 and K=$50, payoff = max(57-50,0) = $7. Subtracting the $4 premium gives a profit of $3. Breakeven for a long call is strike plus premium ($50+$4=$54) — the stock has to rise enough just to recover what was paid for the option before any real profit begins. The $7 payoff splits into $7 of intrinsic value (what the option is worth if exercised right now) and, at expiration, zero time value, since time value has fully decayed by then.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always separate payoff from profit in my head before doing any math — payoff is just what the option is worth at that instant, profit is payoff minus whatever you paid for the right in the first place. Here the option's $7 in the money, so payoff is $7, but you paid $4 for it, so you actually pocket $3. People sometimes assume any in-the-money option is automatically a win, but if the premium you paid was close to or above the payoff, you can be in the money and still underwater. Breakeven is the number I'd quote first in a trading context — $54 here — because that's the level that actually matters for deciding whether the position was worth putting on.
questions.example: S=$57, K=$50, premium=$4. Payoff = max(57-50, 0) = $7. Profit = $7 - $4 = $3. Breakeven = $50 + $4 = $54 — the stock needed to clear $54 just to cover the premium.
commonMistakes: Reporting the payoff ($7) as the profit, forgetting to subtract the premium paid
Thinking any in-the-money option is automatically profitable regardless of what was paid for it
Computing breakeven as just the strike price, ignoring the premium
Mixing up the payoff formula for a put (max(K-S,0)) with the call formula
keyPoints: Call payoff = max(S - K, 0); never negative
Profit = payoff minus the premium paid (for the buyer)
Breakeven for a long call = strike + premium
Intrinsic value is the payoff if exercised now; time value is the remainder of the premium, which decays to zero by expiration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes payoff using max(S-K,0)
Correctly distinguishes payoff from profit and subtracts the premium
Correctly identifies breakeven as strike plus premium
Articulates intrinsic vs. time value clearly

questions.title: Put-Call Parity Intuition
questions.prompt: Explain put-call parity in your own words. What does C - P = S - K·e^(-rT) actually say, and why must it hold for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock?
questions.modelAnswer: Put-call parity says a call minus a put on the same underlying, strike, and expiration must equal the stock price minus the present value of the strike. It's derived by building two portfolios with identical payoffs at expiration regardless of where the stock ends up: Portfolio A (long call plus a risk-free bond that grows to K) and Portfolio B (long put plus long stock). Both portfolios pay off exactly max(S,K) at expiration in every scenario, so by no-arbitrage they must cost the same today, which rearranges to C - P = S - K·e^(-rT). It holds not because of any assumption about how the stock moves, but purely because two things with identical future payoffs must have identical prices today — if they didn't, you could sell the expensive side, buy the cheap side, and lock in a riskless profit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of parity as a sanity check more than a pricing model — it doesn't tell you what the call or put should individually be worth, only that if you know one, you know the other, given the stock price and the discounted strike. If a desk ever quotes a call and a put that violate this relationship, that's not a market view, that's a mispricing, and it gets arbitraged away almost immediately by anyone paying attention. It's also the first thing I'd check if two option prices looked inconsistent with each other before trusting either one.
questions.example: S=$40, K=$40, r=4% continuous, T=0.5 years, call trades at $3.00. Parity says P = C - S + K·e^(-rT) = 3.00 - 40 + 40·e^(-0.02) = 3.00 - 40 + 39.21 = $2.21. If the put is quoted at $2.80 in the market, it's overpriced relative to the call by about $0.59, and an arbitrageur could sell the put, buy the call, short the stock, and lend the proceeds to lock in that gap risk-free.
commonMistakes: Thinking parity only applies when the market is 'wrong' rather than always holding by construction
Forgetting to discount the strike to present value before comparing it to C - P
Applying the formula unmodified to American options, which can be exercised early
Forgetting the formula needs adjustment for a stock that pays dividends
keyPoints: C - P = S - K·e^(-rT) for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock
Derived from two portfolios with identical payoffs: call+bond vs. put+stock
A violation implies a riskless arbitrage, which is why markets keep prices pinned to it
Holds independent of any model of how the stock price moves

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the formula correctly
Explains the replicating-portfolio derivation
Explains why a violation implies arbitrage
Notes the European / no-dividend assumption

questions.title: Pricing a Simple Coupon Bond
questions.prompt: Price a 2-year bond with a $1,000 face value, a 5% annual coupon, and a yield to maturity of 7%. Show your work, and explain why the bond prices below face value.
questions.modelAnswer: Each cash flow is discounted at the 7% yield: Year 1 pays a $50 coupon, discounted to $50/1.07 = $46.73. Year 2 pays the final $50 coupon plus the $1,000 face value, i.e. $1,050, discounted to $1,050/1.07^2 = $1,050/1.1449 = $917.37. Summing gives a price of $46.73 + $917.37 = $964.10. The bond prices below its $1,000 face value because its coupon rate (5%) is below the market's required yield (7%) — a buyer paying face value would only earn 5%, so the price has to fall until the bond's total return (coupon income plus price appreciation to face value at maturity) equals 7%.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always work it cash flow by cash flow rather than trying to shortcut it, especially under interview pressure — write down every payment date, discount each one back at the yield, and add them up. The 'why below face value' part is really just: coupon rate below yield means the market is attaching a value to future cash flows that's below what those cash flows deliver on paper, so the price has to give the buyer the rest of their return through capital appreciation to par at maturity.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to add the face value to the final coupon payment in the last period
Discounting every cash flow by the same single period instead of compounding by each year
Confusing the coupon rate with the yield to maturity
Assuming a bond always prices at face value regardless of yield
keyPoints: Bond price = present value of all coupons plus present value of face value
Each cash flow is discounted at the yield to maturity, compounded by its own time period
Coupon rate below yield → price below face value (discount bond)
Coupon rate above yield → price above face value (premium bond)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly discounts each cash flow at the right power of (1+y)
Correctly includes face value in the final period
Arrives at the correct total price (~$964.10)
Explains the discount-to-par intuition

questions.title: Computing a Basic Sharpe Ratio
questions.prompt: A fund has an annualized return of 11%, the risk-free rate is 3%, and the fund's annualized volatility is 16%. Compute its Sharpe ratio. Is that a strong result?
questions.modelAnswer: Sharpe = (0.11 - 0.03) / 0.16 = 0.08 / 0.16 = 0.50. As a rule of thumb, a Sharpe near 1.0 is considered solid for a systematic strategy, above 2.0 is very strong (and worth double-checking for bias), and below 0.5 is considered weak. A Sharpe of exactly 0.50 sits right at that weak/acceptable boundary — it means the fund is being paid relatively little excess return for the volatility it's taking on, and on its own, over a short sample, this single number also carries meaningful estimation uncertainty.
questions.professionalAnswer: 0.5 is the kind of number where I wouldn't call it bad, but I also wouldn't get excited — it's return the fund is earning for its bumpiness, and 0.5 means you're not getting paid all that generously per unit of volatility. Before judging it further I'd want to know the sample length it came from and whether it's net of fees, because a 0.5 computed gross over six months tells you almost nothing, while the same number over ten years net of fees is a much more informative result.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract the risk-free rate before dividing by volatility
Using return and volatility measured over different periods (e.g. monthly return, annual volatility) without converting
Treating any positive Sharpe as automatically 'good' without a rule-of-thumb benchmark
Not asking what sample length or net/gross basis the ratio was computed over
keyPoints: Sharpe = excess return over the risk-free rate, divided by total volatility
A Sharpe near 1.0 is generally considered solid; below 0.5 is weak
A single Sharpe number needs its sample period and net/gross basis stated to be meaningful

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes Sharpe = 0.50
Correctly characterizes 0.50 relative to standard rules of thumb
Notes the need for sample period / gross-vs-net context

questions.title: Spotting a Survivorship-Bias Mistake
questions.prompt: A junior analyst backtests a 'buy the S&P 500' strategy back to 2005 by pulling today's list of S&P 500 constituents and assuming that list applied the whole time. What's wrong with this, and what should they do instead?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a textbook survivorship bias mistake: using today's index membership and applying it retroactively silently excludes every company that was in the S&P 500 at some point since 2005 but has since been delisted, gone bankrupt, or been acquired. Because the companies that disappear from an index are, on average, the worst performers, a backtest built this way systematically overstates the historical return of holding 'the S&P 500' at any given point in the past. The fix is to use a point-in-time universe — a historical record of which companies were actually members of the index on each date being tested — so that the backtest includes the eventual losers and not just the survivors that happen to still be in the index today.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of the first things I check when I'm handed someone else's backtest — ask exactly how the universe was built. If the answer is 'I pulled the current constituent list,' that's an immediate red flag regardless of how good the numbers look, because every stock that got removed for underperforming or going under is just missing from the test. It's an easy mistake to make because current constituent lists are the easy, free data to get, and point-in-time membership data usually costs more or takes more work to source.
commonMistakes: Assuming index membership is static and doesn't change over time
Treating 'current constituents' and 'point-in-time constituents' as interchangeable
Not realizing that acquisitions are a partial exception (often a positive outcome for the acquired company's shareholders) worth separating from outright delistings/bankruptcies
Fixing the universe but still carrying other look-ahead issues, like using restated fundamental data
keyPoints: Survivorship bias excludes historical failures by building the universe from today's survivors
Companies that disappear from an index are disproportionately the underperformers
The fix is point-in-time index membership, not a static current list
This bias always inflates backtested performance, never deflates it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names the problem as survivorship bias
Explains why it inflates (not deflates) backtested returns
Proposes point-in-time universe membership as the fix
Notes the acquisition vs. delisting nuance

questions.title: Why Diversification Reduces Risk
questions.prompt: Explain why combining two imperfectly correlated assets in a portfolio produces less risk than the simple weighted average of their individual risks. What happens as correlation approaches 1, and what happens as it approaches -1?
questions.modelAnswer: A two-asset portfolio's variance has a cross term, 2·w1·w2·ρ·σ1·σ2, in addition to each asset's own weighted variance. As long as correlation ρ is below 1, that cross term is smaller than it would be if the assets moved in lockstep, which makes the combined portfolio's standard deviation come out below the simple weighted average of the two individual standard deviations — that gap is the diversification benefit. As ρ approaches 1, the cross term grows and the benefit shrinks toward zero: two perfectly correlated assets provide no diversification at all, and portfolio volatility becomes exactly the weighted average. As ρ approaches -1, the cross term becomes strongly negative, and it's possible to construct a combination where the two assets' moves offset almost completely, driving portfolio volatility toward a much smaller number — in the limit, a perfectly hedged, nearly risk-free combination.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd explain this to someone without the formula in front of them: risk doesn't just add up when you combine assets, because what matters is how often they move against each other, not just how much each one moves on its own. Two assets that are highly correlated basically behave like one bigger position — you haven't actually spread your risk, you've just made the same bet bigger. The real diversification benefit only shows up when you hold things that genuinely don't move together, and the lower that correlation gets, the more the portfolio's volatility falls below what a naive weighted average would suggest.
questions.example: With σ1=20%, σ2=30%, ρ=0.3, w1=w2=0.5: portfolio volatility comes out to about 20.4%, well below the 25% simple average of 20% and 30% — that 4.6-point gap is pure diversification benefit from the assets not being perfectly correlated.
commonMistakes: Assuming portfolio risk is simply the weighted average of individual asset risks
Forgetting the cross term in the two-asset variance formula entirely
Believing diversification eliminates all risk rather than only unsystematic risk
Confusing covariance (scale-dependent) with correlation (normalized, -1 to +1)
keyPoints: Portfolio variance includes a correlation-dependent cross term, not just weighted individual variances
Lower correlation produces a bigger diversification benefit
At ρ=1, there is no diversification benefit; at ρ=-1, risk can be nearly eliminated
Diversification only reduces unsystematic (asset-specific) risk, not market-wide systematic risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States and explains the two-asset variance formula with its cross term
Correctly describes the ρ→1 case (no benefit)
Correctly describes the ρ→-1 case (risk near-elimination)
Notes the limit (systematic risk remains regardless)

questions.title: Explaining VaR to a Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: A business unit head who isn't quantitative asks you what 'our 1-day 99% VaR is $2 million' actually means. How do you explain it in plain terms without losing accuracy?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd explain it as: on a typical day, we don't expect to lose anywhere near $2 million, but on roughly 1 out of every 100 trading days, we'd expect a loss that exceeds $2 million — it's a threshold, not a worst case. I'd be explicit that it does not mean $2 million is the most we could ever lose; it means losses bigger than that are supposed to be rare, specifically a 1-in-100-day event, and that the number is only meaningful with both the confidence level (99%) and horizon (1 day) attached, since 'VaR is $2 million' alone, without those two pieces, is an incomplete statement.
questions.professionalAnswer: I try to get across two things in under a minute: it's a threshold, not a ceiling, and it's silent about how bad the bad day actually gets. I'll usually say something like, 'think of it as a weather forecast for a 1-in-100-day storm — it tells you how often we'd expect to see a loss past this line, not how deep the worst flood could get.' If they push further I'll bring up Expected Shortfall as the number that actually answers 'how bad does it get on those bad days,' since that's usually their next question anyway.
commonMistakes: Describing VaR as the maximum possible loss
Omitting the confidence level or time horizon when stating the number
Implying VaR says anything about how severe a loss beyond the threshold would be
Using jargon like 'quantile of the P&L distribution' without translating it
keyPoints: VaR is a threshold not expected to be exceeded with a given confidence, over a given horizon
It is not the worst-case or maximum possible loss
Both the confidence level and horizon must be stated for the number to be meaningful
VaR says nothing about severity beyond the threshold — that's what Expected Shortfall is for

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives an accurate, jargon-free plain-language explanation
Explicitly corrects the 'maximum loss' misconception
Mentions the confidence level and horizon as necessary context
Connects to Expected Shortfall as the natural follow-up

questions.title: Why a Quantitative Analyst Role
questions.prompt: How do you describe the quantitative analyst role, and what distinguishes it from a quant researcher or quant trader role at the same firm?
questions.modelAnswer: A quant analyst sits closer to the business and risk side than a quant researcher or quant trader: the role is about translating market behavior, pricing, and risk into decisions and reports other people act on — things like pricing a position, measuring a portfolio's risk exposures, running performance attribution, or building a stress-testing or valuation framework — rather than originating new trading signals (researcher) or executing and managing live positions in real time (trader). A quant researcher leans heaviest on statistics and model-building to find an edge; a quant trader leans heaviest on market intuition and decisiveness under live conditions; a quant analyst leans on translating quantitative finance into clear, defensible analysis for traders, portfolio managers, and risk committees.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd put it this way: the researcher is trying to find the edge, the trader is running it live, and the analyst is making sure everyone understands what the position is actually exposed to and why it's performing the way it is. I'm drawn to that translation layer — I like being able to go deep on the Greeks, the risk model, or the attribution numbers, but ultimately produce something a PM or a risk committee can act on without needing to rebuild my analysis themselves.
commonMistakes: Describing all three roles (researcher, trader, analyst) as interchangeable
Focusing only on technical skills without explaining what the role actually produces day to day
Overclaiming trading-desk decision authority that an analyst role typically doesn't have
Giving a generic 'I like math and markets' answer without specifics
keyPoints: Quant analyst: translates pricing, risk, and performance analysis into decisions for traders/PMs/risk committees
Quant researcher: designs and backtests signals/models, heaviest on statistics
Quant trader: executes and manages live risk, heaviest on market intuition and speed
Role lines blur more at smaller firms than at large ones

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clearly distinguishes analyst from researcher and trader roles
Gives concrete examples of analyst deliverables (risk reports, attribution, pricing analysis)
Shows genuine, specific motivation rather than a generic answer
